reader_access_routes: Committee of Public Safety: authority and limits
findings.analytical_note: The Committee mobilized leadership without initially becoming an undisputed government. War reverses, internal revolt and contested Parisian power formed the setting for its expansion.

Federalist retreat varied by place. Bordeaux’s propaganda, mint seizure and hostile reception of emissaries produced demands for harsher treatment than northern centers, even after formal dissolution of its rebel commission.

Marseilles divided over seeking British help; refugees’ atrocity reports helped push Toulon toward accepting royalist conditions and enemy protection. These were contingent escalations, not the original aims of the urban rebels.

Rivals competed for Marat’s constituency and adopted similar demands for expanded controls, revolutionary armies and punishment. Distinguish organizational rivalry from a sharply different economic doctrine.

Subsistence discontent and news of Toulon opened an opportunity for organized pressure. The Convention granted revolutionary armies, faster justice and paid twice-weekly meetings; official conscription was narrower than demands for universal enlistment.
Broad suspicion criteria made ordinary language and insufficient zeal dangerous. Emergency price controls and organized coercion developed together, but are separate institutional mechanisms.
The ascendant radicals first silenced their radical rivals. Democratic constitutional implementation was explicitly deferred, and temporary emergency government justified central direction.

Famous trials marked the Terror but do not represent its social or geographic majority. Robespierre impeded some prosecutions and protected protest-signing deputies, complicating indiscriminate personal attribution.
Paris demanded exemplary destruction and punishment after protracted resistance. Couthon recoiled; successors intensified courts and used mass gunfire when the guillotine could not meet the pace.

Loss of commanding heights forced allied evacuation; refugees escaped, but mass shootings and commission trials followed. Strategic naval value limited further destruction despite the scale of perceived betrayal.

Relatively high acquittal rates and lower executions distinguished Marseilles and Bordeaux from Lyons and Toulon. Bordeaux repression intensified under Jullien when it was already declining in much of the country.

Repatriated regular troops and Parisian forces pursued devastation, with uneven success. Rebel localism prevented exploitation of victories; defeat at Cholet triggered the march toward a hoped-for British link.

The absence of timely British aid and siege equipment doomed Granville. Blocked recrossing of the Loire, rout and systematic pursuit destroyed the main army, including many accompanying noncombatants.
Destruction continued after the main army’s defeat, with indiscriminate killings and demographic consequences. The author offers a debated scale of deaths rather than a precise settled total.

Mass drowning and shooting accompanied exceptional judicial repression in the Vendée region. Carrier’s earlier moderation, local fear of rebel massacres and few Nantes-born victims complicate a purely personal-sadism account without excusing actions.
Recall arose amid central concern that excesses made enemies and local efforts to transfer blame. Investigation and centralization must be distinguished from later retrospective trials.
Local urban artisans supplied knowledge for coercion and provisioning. The full human cost includes imprisonment, custodial mortality and undocumented killing, beyond formal death sentences.

Victims concentrated in rebellion and frontier areas; ordinary people predominated although elites were disproportionately affected. The author separates official counts, broader estimates excluding Vendée, and comparisons with other European killings.

Fouché’s experience of Vendéan religious mobilization underlay suppression even of constitutional Catholicism and replacement with civic morality. Local initiative in an otherwise quiet district shaped a wider movement.

Calendar reform and unsolicited local campaigns interacted. Demolition, appropriation of metal and mock ceremonies combined ideological and war-supply purposes; coercion reached clergy previously loyal to the Revolution.
Official symbolic changes and ceremonies elevated Paris’s example, while Grégoire retained his religious office and dress. Festival of Reason and later Supreme Being cult should not be conflated.

Persecution endangered order and provisioning; Robespierre defended socially necessary religious belief. Formal protection of worship did not immediately stop church closures or coerced renunciations, whose chronology varied locally.

The law established reporting chains and prohibited local reinterpretation, bypassed departments for emergency functions, and suppressed unofficial bodies. Implementation was gradual and resisted; constitutional decentralization remained an ideal deferred to peace.

Local 1790 price bases created uneven incentives; transport and profit adjustments followed. Wage limits were scarcely enforced initially, black markets persisted and military buying competed with controls; central schedules nevertheless expanded practical regulation.

Reduced currency demand under controls and removal of assignats through the forced loan helped stabilization. A punitive-looking income levy could be paid in depreciated paper, and implementation varied.
Sequestration and redistribution proposals had limited, chaotic application. Colleagues’ lukewarm support and the wish to outbid radicals qualify any account of an achieved social revolution.

Military recovery opened pressure for restraint, but criticism itself risked suspicion. Initial cooperation between Danton and Robespierre makes subsequent factional alignments contingent rather than fixed.

Real corruption and a real royalist intriguer were woven into a much broader alleged foreign plot. Discovery of Fabre’s corruption broke Robespierre’s confidence in the Indulgents; preserve the difference between evidence and inferred conspiracy.

Vincent and Ronsin: arrest and release
findings.analytical_note: Counterattacks over Lyons halted moderation and polarized governing committees. Release for lack of evidence did not end personal vengeance or political conflict.

A poorly organized appeal failed to mobilize other sections. Committees used predetermined political prosecution and famine/foreign-plot allegations to destroy opponents; accusations should not be recorded as proven operational plans.

Programmatic concessions, fatigue and incorporation of experienced activists into paid administration weakened independent mobilization. The source offers several reinforcing explanations for abandonment of Hébertists, not just repression.

Purges and dissolution ended independent popular instruments without ending Terror. The chapter explicitly warns that centralized repression would grow worse after its supposed popular authors disappeared.

qualifications: Mortality figures are retained as estimates with different geographic and procedural denominators, not combined into one exact total.
The source attributes broad conspiracy claims to contemporaries while separately substantiating narrower corruption; no outside adjudication is imported.
